kits.familyName: Comparing possible fixes before choosing one
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and the team is choosing between possible fixes for a recurring problem.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are asked to help compare fixes for a problem the team keeps having.
detail: It is the middle of the afternoon.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is not worth the trouble.
You are in a hurry to finish.

tiers.1: A fix must keep every safety feature in place.
tiers.2: A set budget is a firm limit on what can be chosen.
tiers.3: A fix that treats the cause beats one that hides the symptom.
tiers.4: An untried fix gets a small trial before it is used everywhere.
tiers.5: When fixes look equal, the evidence decides.

fact: Two fixes would speed up packing, but one removes a safety guard, and {lead|the} says fixes must keep every safety feature.
issues.short: the fix that removes the guard
issues.action: Choose the fix that keeps the guard in place.
issues.brief: choose the fix that keeps the guard
issues.reason: A fix that removes protection solves one problem by creating a more serious one.
issues.lesson: Rule out fixes that remove safety features before comparing anything else.

shortcut.text: Choose the faster fix, since speed is the goal.
shortcut.why: Speed does not outweigh the safety feature, and {lead|the} has said fixes must keep it.
shortcut.mis: The goal of a fix is the only thing that matters.

clear: The team already dropped the fix that removes the guard.
issues.done: the guard-removing fix is already ruled out

fact: Three fixes would stop a leak, {lead|the} set a budget of $200, and one fix costs $350.
issues.action: Choose among the fixes that fit the $200 budget.
issues.reason: A fix over the budget cannot be bought, so it is not a real choice.
issues.lesson: Keep to the limits that are set before you compare fixes.

shortcut.text: Choose the $350 fix, since it is the most thorough.
shortcut.why: The budget is a limit, and a fix that cannot be paid for does not solve the problem.
shortcut.mis: The most thorough fix is always the best.

clear: The $350 fix was already ruled out for going over the budget.
issues.done: the over-budget fix is already ruled out

fact: A printer jams every day, one fix only clears the jam, and another fixes why the paper keeps catching.
issues.action: Choose the fix that stops the paper from catching.
issues.brief: choose the fix that treats the cause
issues.reason: A fix that treats the cause stops the problem returning, while clearing jams only hides it.
issues.lesson: Prefer a fix that treats the cause of a repeating problem.

shortcut.text: Choose the quick fix and clear the jams as they happen.
shortcut.why: The jams will keep coming back, and each one takes time again.
shortcut.mis: A quick fix is the same as a solution.

clear: The team already chose the fix that stops the paper from catching.
issues.done: the cause-treating fix is already chosen

fact: A fix has not been tried before, and {lead|the} says untried fixes get a small trial first.
issues.action: Run a small trial of the fix first.
issues.reason: A small trial shows whether the fix works and what it changes, before everyone depends on it.
issues.lesson: Try an untested fix on a small scale before using it widely.

shortcut.text: Use it everywhere now, since it should work.
shortcut.why: Problems then appear everywhere at once, and the guide wants a trial first.
shortcut.mis: If it should work, it will work.

clear: The untried fix already passed a small trial.

fact: Two fixes look equal, but the log shows one would have prevented 8 of last month's 10 problems, the other 2.
issues.short: the choice between two equal-looking fixes
issues.action: Choose the fix that addresses most of the logged problems.
issues.brief: choose the fix that addresses the most logged problems
issues.reason: The log shows which fix would have helped most, which is better than how the fixes look.
issues.lesson: Use the evidence you have to choose between fixes that look similar.

shortcut.text: Choose whichever fix is easier to explain.
shortcut.why: Ease of explaining does not show which fix would help more.
shortcut.mis: The simplest explanation is the best fix.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves comparing fixes before choosing one.
proceed.lesson: Compare fixes against safety, limits, causes, trials and evidence before choosing one.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the written guide, and it may be out of date.
generic.mis: Common practice is the same as the rule.

generic.text: Wait until {lead|the} brings it up before you act.
generic.why: The guide applies to you now, and waiting leaves the problem in place.
generic.mis: Someone else will raise it if it matters.

overcaution.text: Refuse to choose any fix until every possible fix has been tested.
overcaution.why: The point is to choose with the information you have. Testing everything delays the fix.
overcaution.mis: A choice needs every option tested.

setup: The team needs to choose a fix for a repeating problem.

steps.text: Write down the safety and budget limits
Compare the fixes against the limits and the evidence

rel: Compare fixes against the limits you wrote down.
You compare fixes you have listed.
process.lesson: Write the limits, list the fixes, compare them, then choose one to trial.

title: Notes on choosing a fix
intro: You are reading a coworker's draft advice on choosing between fixes.
prompt: Which line gives advice that leads to a poor choice?
doc.lesson: A good choice compares fixes against safety, budget, cause and evidence.

lines.text: Rule out fixes that remove safety features.

bad.text: Pick the fastest fix even if it removes a safety feature.
bad.why: A fix that removes protection creates a worse problem.

lines.text: Keep to the budget set for the fix.

bad.text: Pick the most thorough fix even if it goes over the budget.
bad.why: A fix that cannot be paid for is not an option.

lines.text: Prefer the fix that treats the cause.

bad.text: Prefer the quick fix that clears each problem as it appears.

lines.text: Try an untested fix on a small scale first.

review.notes: Everyday decision-making only; no named method or framework. Tiers: safety, budget, cause, trial, evidence.
